# The provenance file on Luxor

*Catalogue entry — Luxor. Every claim below carries its chain of custody.*

## Provenance

**1. The attestation.** **—**, from the tradition's own record. On record: Luxor temple birth-colonnade reliefs (Amenhotep III), Opet festival reliefs and barque-docking scenes, Abu Haggag mouloud tradition, Haeny, Luxor in the Oxford Encyclopedia of Ancient Egypt.

**2. The narrative record.** **The Southern Journey** — The Opet festival’s climax was the god’s arrival at Ipet-resyt: the barque of Amun moored before the colonnade, the Theban crowd celebrating the union that renewed the Nile, the king, and the year in a single night of liturgy.  The return to Karnak closed the cycle eleven days later. **Amun and Mutemwiya** — Luxor’s colonnade reliefs narrate the conception of Amenhotep III: Amun takes the form of the king, visits queen Mutemwiya, the child is fashioned by Khnum on the potter’s wheel and blessed by the gods — the canonical statement that the pharaoh is the god’s literal son, carved at full scale.

**3. The physical record.** Amenhotep III’s colonnade and court survive at near-perfect scale; the pylon of Ramesses II fronts it with its single obelisk — the other stands in Paris’ Place de la Concorde. The temple’s axis was recently realigned with the re-excavated Avenue of Sphinxes to Karnak, restoring the ancient processional road.

**4. The current holding.** The temple at [/luxor/](/luxor/), a temple of the restored name. aSCII-equivalent form

**5. The documented resonances.** **Travel, Tourism & Place Branding**, **Wedding, Family & Maternity**, **Architecture & Spatial Design** — seats argued and weighted in the [pattern atlas](/patterns/), read through the myths in this temple's [Resonance File](/luxor/blog/resonance/).

**6. The primary sources.** [The Book of the Dead](/texts/book-of-the-dead/) — the library this file answers to, open at the [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/).

**7. The continuing record.** The colonnade of Amenhotep III, floodlit on the Nile’s corniche, is the most photographed temple front in the world after the Pyramids.  The birth-colonnade’s iconography — Khnum at the potter’s wheel, the divine child — became the standard visual argument of Egyptian kingship, copied in every royal birth-chapel of the New Kingdom.
